Hermite Polynomials & Wiener Chaos
text:
Chaos Decomposition
The representation of \(f(X)\) in terms of Hermite polynomials forms a stochastic series known as the Wiener Chaos Expansion:
\[
f(X) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}_X[f^{(n)}(X)]}{n!} H_n(X)
\]
The expansion coefficients can be generated directly via the exponential generating function:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}_X[f(X)e^{\lambda X - \frac{1}{2}\lambda^2}] &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}_X[f(X)H_n(X)] \\
    &= \sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}\mathbb{E}_X[f^{(n)}(X)] \\
    &= \mathbb{E}_X[f(X+\lambda)]
\end{align*}
\]
where the final line follows from the Taylor expansion of \(f(X + \lambda)\) in expectation. The first term is the mean \(\mathbb{E}_X[f(X)H_0(X)] = \mathbb{E}_X[f(X)]\), while the second term accounts for how the scale of variation in \(X_t\) affects drift (e.g., \(\mathbb{E}[f(B_t)\sigma_t B_t] = \sigma_t t \mathbb{E}[f'(B_t)]\)).
This shift interpretation generalizes directly to Girsanov’s Theorem.

title: Hermite Polynomials & Wiener Chaos
text:
Girsanov’s Theorem
Consider a homogeneous diffusion process \(X_t\) satisfying:
\[
X_t = \int_{t=0}^T \mu(t,X_t) \mathrm{d}t + \int_{t=0}^T \mathrm{d}B_t
\]
where \(B_t\) is a standard Brownian motion. Girsanov’s Theorem states that:
\[
\mathcal{E}_t = \exp\left(X_t - \frac{1}{2}[X]_t\right)
\]
where \([X]_t\) is the quadratic variation, is a martingale representing the likelihood ratio under measure transformation.
To “subtract off” the drift so that only the Brownian motion component remains, Girsanov’s Theorem establishes:
\[
\mathbb{E}_{X_t}[f(X_t)] = \mathbb{E}_{B_t}\left[f(B_t) e^{\int_{t=0}^T \mu(t,X_t)\mathrm{d}B_t - \frac{1}{2}\int_{t=0}^T \mu(t,X_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t}\right]
\]
Equivalently, defining \(\tilde{B}_t = B_t + \int_0^t \mu(s,X_s)\mathrm{d}s\) converts \(X_t\) into a Brownian motion under measure \(Q\):
\[
\int_{t=0}^T \mu(t,X_t) \mathrm{d}t + \int_{t=0}^T \mathrm{d}B_t = \int_{t=0}^T \mu(t,X_t) \mathrm{d}t + \int_{t=0}^T \mathrm{d}\left(\tilde{B}_t - \int_{0}^t \mu(s,X_s)\mathrm{d}s\right) = \int_{t=0}^T \mathrm{d}\tilde{B}_t
\]
When state-dependent volatility \(\sigma(t,X_t) > 0\) is present:
\[
\int_{t=0}^T \mu(t,X_t) \mathrm{d}t + \int_{t=0}^T \sigma(t,X_t) \mathrm{d}B_t = \int_{t=0}^T \sigma(t,X_t)\mathrm{d}\tilde{B}_t
\]
where \(\mathrm{d}\tilde{B}_t = \mathrm{d}B_t + \frac{\mu(t,X_t)}{\sigma(t,X_t)}\mathrm{d}t\) under measure \(Q\), yielding:
\[
\mathbb{E}_{X_t}[f(X_t)] = \mathbb{E}_Q\left[f(X_t)e^{\int_{t=0}^T \frac{\mu(t,X_t)}{\sigma(t,X_t)}\mathrm{d}B_t - \frac{1}{2}\int_{t=0}^T \left( \frac{\mu(t,X_t)}{\sigma(t,X_t)} \right)^2 \mathrm{d}t}\right]
\]

Summary: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Initial Example and Calculations
To illustrate the framework, consider approximating a target process such as Brownian motion \(W_t\) over a time horizon \([0, T]\). Define the objective functional:
\[
\mathcal{J}[X(\sigma)] = \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (W_t^2 - X_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t\right]
\]
which measures the expected squared deviation between \(X_t\) and the path \(W_t^2\).
Suppose \(X_t\) belongs to a class of pure diffusion processes:
\[
X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \sigma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
We examine the first variation \(\delta \mathcal{J}\) under a perturbation \(\sigma \mapsto \sigma + \varepsilon \gamma\), where \(\gamma_t\) is a suitably regular stochastic process vanishing on boundaries:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \delta \mathcal{J}[X(\sigma)] &= \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (W_t^2 - X_t + \varepsilon \tilde{X}_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t\right] - \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (W_t^2 - X_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t\right] \right) \\
    &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T 2(W_t^2 - X_t)\tilde{X}_t \mathrm{d}t \right]
\end{align*}
\]
Expanding the variation process \(\tilde{X}_t\):
\[
\delta \mathcal{J}[X(\sigma)] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T 2(W_t^2 - X_t) \left(\int_0^t \gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s \right) \mathrm{d}t \right]
\]
To express this variation as an inner product, we introduce the Skorohod integral operator \(\delta(\cdot)\), formally written using white noise \(\dot{W}_s\) and Wick product \(\diamond\) (Gjessing et al. 1992):
\[
\delta(\cdot) = \int_0^T (\cdot)\diamond \dot{W}_s \mathrm{d}s = \int_0^T (\cdot) \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
Using the Malliavin integration-by-parts duality under Gaussian measure (Nualart 2019):
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[ F \cdot \delta(u) \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T (\mathbf{D}_s F) u_s \mathrm{d}s \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \langle\mathbf{D}_s F, u \rangle_{[0,T]} \right]
\]
where \(\mathbf{D}_s\) denotes the Malliavin derivative operator. Differentiating diffusion processes yields:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_T = \mathbf{D}_s \int_{0}^T \mu(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}r = \int_{s}^T \mathbf{D}_s \mu(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}r
\]
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_T = \mathbf{D}_s \int_{0}^T \sigma(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r = \sigma(s,X_s) + \int_{s}^T \mathbf{D}_s \sigma(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r
\]
For monomial path evaluations \(W_t^n\):
\[
\mathbf{D}_s (W_t^n) = n W_t^{n-1} \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]
Rewriting \(\tilde{X}_t = \delta\left(\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\gamma\right)\), the functional derivative becomes:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \delta \mathcal{J} &= \int_0^T 2\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T \mathbf{D}_s (W_t^2 - X_t) \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}s\right] \mathrm{d}t \\
    &= \int_0^T 2\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T (2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) - \mathbf{D}_s X_t) \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}s\right] \mathrm{d}t \\
    &= \int_0^T 2\mathbb{E}\left[ \langle 2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) - \mathbf{D}_s X_t, \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\gamma \rangle\right] \mathrm{d}t
\end{align*}
\]
Stationarity requires:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^t \mathbf{D}_s\sigma(r,X_r)\mathrm{d}W_r = 2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]


Note that setting \(\sigma(s,X_s) = 2 W_s \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\) formally satisfies this relation, but makes \(\sigma\) explicitly path-dependent via \(W_s\) rather than a deterministic state function \(\sigma(s,x)\).

Polynomial & Hermite Expansions
When restricting \(X_t\) to finite Hermite polynomial expansions:
\[
X_t = \sum_{n=0}^N c_n H_n \left(\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right)
\]
the Malliavin derivative simplifies to:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{c_n}{\sqrt{t}} H_{n-1} \left(\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right)
\]
Since Hermite polynomials form an orthonormal basis on Wiener space (Gjessing et al. 1992; Nualart 2019), the coefficients satisfy:
\[
c_n = \langle F, H_n\rangle_{\Omega} = \mathbb{E}[F H_n] = \mathbb{E}[\partial^n_x F]
\]
When coefficients are time-dependent (\(c_n \doteq c_n(t)\)), the Skorohod integral takes the Wick product form:
\[
\delta\left(c_n(t) H_n \left(\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right) \right) = \int_0^T \left(\frac{c_n(t)}{t^{n/2}}W^{\diamond n}_t\right) \diamond \dot{W}_t \mathrm{d}t
\]
For general diffusions with drift \(\mu(r,X_r)\) and volatility \(\sigma(r,X_r)\), the tangent variation process \(Y_r = \mathbf{D}_s X_r\) solves:
\[
\mathrm{d}Y_r = \mu_x (r,X_r)Y_r \mathrm{d}r + \sigma_x (r,X_r) Y_r \mathrm{d}W_r, \quad Y_s = \sigma(s,X_s)
\]
with explicit geometric solution:
\[
Y_t = \sigma(s,X_s)\exp\left\{\int_s^t \left(\mu_x (r,X_r) - \frac{1}{2} \sigma_{x}^2(r,X_r)\right)\mathrm{d}r + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r\right\}
\]

Theorem 1 (Clark-Ocone Formula) Let \(F \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}\) be \(\mathcal{F}_T\)-measurable. Then \(F\) admits the stochastic integral representation (Hairer 2021; Nualart 2019):
\[
F = \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t
\]

Geometric and Manifold Considerations
Key geometric insights regarding this calculus include:

Stationary Conditions vs. Optimization Geometry: While necessary conditions for stationary points can be derived heuristically, equipping the space of diffusion processes with a Riemannian manifold structure (enabling gradient descent) remains difficult.
Variational Spaces: Variations on drift coefficients correspond naturally to the flat geometry of the Cameron-Martin space. However, variations on diffusion coefficients \(\sigma\) lack an obvious metric structure without restricting to specific density-space geometries (e.g., Wasserstein flows) (Lambert et al. 2022).

title: Summary: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Parametric Perturbations
Consider a parameter \(\theta_t\) driving process \(X_t \sim P_{\theta_t}\) with Gaussian prior \(\theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\vartheta_t, \int_0^t v_s \mathrm{d}s\right)\). Representing \(X_t = G^{-1}(t, U, \theta_t)\) via conditional CDF \(G\):
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \left \langle \frac{\sigma_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)}{g(G^{-1}(t,U, \theta_t))}, \dot{\gamma}_s \right \rangle
\]
In Wasserstein geometry, vector fields take the form \(V(\rho) = -\nabla \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta \rho}\) (Lambert et al. 2022). For relative entropy \(\mathcal{F}[\rho] = \mathcal{D}_{KL}(\rho \parallel \rho^*)\), \(V(\rho) = -\left(\frac{\nabla \rho}{\rho} + \nabla f\right)\), corresponding to Langevin diffusion:
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = -\nabla f (X_t) \mathrm{d}t + \sqrt{2} \mathrm{d}W_t
\]
The first variation process for Langevin diffusion evaluates to:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sqrt{2}\exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\}
\]


This indicates that pathwise perturbations decay or amplify exponentially according to accumulated spatial curvature \(\Delta f(X_r)\) along the trajectory.
Applying Girsanov’s Theorem with change of measure \(Z_t = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}P}\Big|_t\):
\[
\frac{1}{2} \langle \mathbf{D}_s V(X_t), (\mathbf{D}_s V)^* (X_t) Z_t\rangle = \left \langle - \partial_t \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r,X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\}, Z_t \right \rangle
\]

title: Summary: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Malliavin Operators on Wiener Space
Let \(\mathbb{F}_t\) denote the \(L^2\)-space of \(\mathcal{F}_t\)-adapted processes generated by Brownian motion (Hairer 2021).

Theorem 2 (Wiener Representation Theorem) Every \(F \in L^2(\Omega, \mathcal{F}_T, P)\) admits a unique representation (Di Nunno et al. 2009; Nualart 2019):
\[
F_T = \mathbb{E}[F_T] + \int_{0}^{T} \alpha^{F}_t \mathrm{d} W_{t}
\]
where \(\alpha^{F}_t\) is an adapted \(L^2\)-predictable process.


Definition 1 (Malliavin Derivative) Let \(F: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a random variable, \(g \in L^2([0,T])\), and \(\gamma(t) = \int_0^t g(s) \mathrm{d}s\). The directional derivative of \(F\) along \(\gamma\) is:
\[
\mathbf{D}_\gamma F(\omega) = \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{F(\omega + \varepsilon \gamma) - F(\omega)}{\varepsilon}
\]
If there exists \(\psi \in L^2([0,T] \times \Omega)\) such that \(\mathbf{D}_\gamma F = \langle \psi, g \rangle_{L^2[0,T]}\), then \(F \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}\) and \(\mathbf{D}_t F = \psi(t, \cdot)\).


Definition 2 (Skorohod Integral (Divergence Operator)) The Skorohod integral operator \(\delta\) is defined as the \(L^2\)-adjoint of the Malliavin derivative \(\mathbf{D}\) (Nualart 2019):
\[
\mathbb{E}[F \cdot \delta(u)] = \mathbb{E}\left[\langle \mathbf{D} F, u \rangle_{L^2[0,T]}\right], \quad \forall F \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}, \, u \in \text{Dom}(\delta)
\]

For adapted processes \(u_t\), \(\delta(u) = \int_0^T u_t \mathrm{d}W_t\) coincides with the Itô integral (Di Nunno et al. 2009). For simple non-adapted processes \(u = \sum_{i=1}^n F_i h_i\):
\[
\delta(u) = \sum_{i=1}^n F_i W(h_i) - \sum_{i=1}^n \langle \mathbf{D} F_i, h_i \rangle_{L^2[0,T]}
\]
Hermite polynomials \(H_n(x)\) arise directly via repeated divergence operations: \(H_n(x) = \delta^n(1)\) (Gjessing et al. 1992). The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck generator \(\Delta = -\delta \mathbf{D}\) satisfies:
\[
\Delta H_n = -n H_n
\]

title: Summary: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Chaos Expansions & Wick Calculus
Iterated stochastic integrals \(I_n(f_n) = \int_0^T \dots \int_0^{t_2} f_n(t_1, \dots, t_n) \mathrm{d}W_{t_1} \dots \mathrm{d}W_{t_n}\) satisfy \(I_n(g^{\otimes n}) = \|g\|^n H_n\left(\frac{\int g \mathrm{d}W}{\|g\|}\right)\) (Gjessing et al. 1992; Nualart 2019).

Definition 3 (Wick Product) For chaos expansions \(X = \sum_{\alpha} x_\alpha H_\alpha\) and \(Y = \sum_{\beta} y_\beta H_\beta\), the Wick product is (Gjessing et al. 1992):
\[
X \diamond Y = \sum_{\gamma} \left(\sum_{\alpha + \beta = \gamma} x_\alpha y_\beta \right) H_{\gamma}
\]

Using Wick products, the SDE \(\mathrm{d}X_t = f(X_t)\mathrm{d}t + \sigma(X_t)\mathrm{d}W_t\) transforms into a random ordinary differential equation (Di Nunno et al. 2009):
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} X_t = f(X_t) + \sigma(X_t) \diamond \dot{W}_t
\]

Example 1 (Geometric Brownian Motion in Wick Form) Geometric Brownian Motion \(\mathrm{d}X_t = \mu X_t \mathrm{d}t + \sigma X_t \mathrm{d}W_t\) written in Wick ODE form:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} X_t = X_t \diamond (\mu + \sigma \dot{W}_t)
\]
has the exact solution:
\[
X_t = x_0 \exp(\mu t) \diamond \exp^{\diamond}(\sigma W_t) = x_0 \exp\left(\left(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)t + \sigma W_t\right)
\]

A failed but interesting log of notes and exploratory calculations on extending PDE-constrained optimization principles to SDEs, covering functional derivatives of diffusions, Malliavin calculus, Skorohod integration, Wick products, and Wasserstein flows. Our first observation is that the idea of using Malliavin based optimization strange, where drift control us trivial (geometrically flat; Cameron-Martin Space; maintains a.c. with respect to original measure; Girsanov’s Theorem) and diffusion control nonsensical (singular; anticipating control). A more interesting observation is made later, where we can show that Malliavin perturbations of a Langevin flow expand or shrink exponentially with the integrated curvature.

Initial Example and Calculations (nonsense!)
To outline a success (which will not be achieved), we would like to demonstrate something like the obvious fact that a Brownian Bridge Process or Gaussian process “best” approximates true Brownian motion given a selection of measurements.
For example, consider the functional:
\[
\mathcal{J}[X(\sigma)] = \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (W_t^2 - X_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t\right]
\]
which can be seen as minimizing the expected squared variation of our process \(X_t\) in comparison to the square Wiener Process (Brownian motion) \(W_t^2\).
Let’s say that \(X_t\) is from some class of diffusion processes of the very simple form:
\[
X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \sigma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
We would now like to ask, what is the variation in this functional \(\mathcal{J}[\sigma, \cdot]\) as we perturb \(\sigma\)? The simplest answer comes from Itô, but let’s calculate this in the more general sense for now by perturbing \(\sigma\) by \(\varepsilon \gamma_t\), where \(\gamma_t\) is a stochastic process with sufficiently nice properties (compact support, vanishing on the boundary, etc.):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \delta \mathcal{J}[X(\sigma)] &= \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (W_t^2 - X_t + \varepsilon \tilde{X}_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t\right] - \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (W_t^2 - X_t)^2 \mathrm{d}t\right] \right) \\
    &= \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T 2(W_t^2 - X_t)\tilde{X}_t \mathrm{d}t \right]
\end{align*}
\]
Expanding \(\tilde{X}_t = \int_0^t \gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s\) as a strictly stochastic term (a perturbation a.c. with respect to \(W_s\)), we have:
\[
\delta \mathcal{J}[X(\sigma)] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T 2(W_t^2 - X_t) \left(\int_0^t \gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s \right) \mathrm{d}t \right]
\]
We now look to express this as an inner product on some space, and look for the “adjoint” that gets rid of this “stochastic integral operator”:
\[
\delta(\cdot) = \int_0^T (\cdot)\diamond \dot{W}_s \mathrm{d}s = \int_0^T (\cdot) \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
The first equality for now is just fancy notation for what a physicist might want to write, and the second equality corresponds to how it appears in the above equation (the explicit “truth” of this will be discussed later) (Gjessing et al. 1992).
We would like to now write everything as an inner product, and identify an adjoint, but as this is motivation and not explicit, you will need to take my word for some of the following calculations which is just a consequence of integration by parts using Stein’s Formula under the Gaussian measure (Nualart 2019).
Here we will identify the adjoint in the sense that for a stochastic process \(\Delta\):
\[
\mathbb{E}\left[ \Delta \delta(\gamma) \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T (\mathbf{D}_t \Delta_T) \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \right] = \mathbb{E}\left[ \langle \mathbf{D}_t \Delta, \gamma \rangle_{[0,T]} \right]
\]
and you will need to take the following properties of this “Stochastic Derivative” \(\mathbf{D}_t\) for granted. When we take the derivative of a diffusion process (where the second line is the supposed form of \(X_T\)), we have:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_T = \mathbf{D}_s \int_{0}^T \mu(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}r = \int_{s}^T \mathbf{D}_s \mu(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}r
\]
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_T = \mathbf{D}_s \int_{0}^T \sigma(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r = \sigma(s,X_s) + \int_{s}^T \mathbf{D}_s \sigma(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r
\]
We will also be using the special case below:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s (W_t^n) = n W_t^{n-1} \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]
Therefore, if we are to rewrite \(\tilde{X}_t\) in terms of this new \(\delta(\cdot)\), we have:
\[
\int_0^t \gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s = \int_0^T \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}W_s = \delta\left(\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\gamma\right)
\]
and further our functional derivative, using the formal notation above, is then:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T 2(W_t^2 - X_t) \delta (\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\gamma) \mathrm{d}t \right] &= \int_0^T \mathbb{E}\left[2(W_t^2 - X_t) \delta (\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\gamma)\right] \mathrm{d}t  \\
    &= \int_0^T 2\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T \mathbf{D}_s (W_t^2 - X_t) \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}s\right] \mathrm{d}t \\
    &= \int_0^T 2\mathbb{E}\left[ \int_0^T (2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) - \mathbf{D}_s X_t) \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\gamma(s,X_s) \mathrm{d}s\right] \mathrm{d}t \\
    &= \int_0^T 2\mathbb{E}\left[ \langle (2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) - \mathbf{D}_s X_t), \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\gamma \rangle\right] \mathrm{d}t
\end{align*}
\]
And we come to the obvious conclusion that the \(\sigma(t,X_t)\) minimizing the square variation over time must have:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^T \mathbf{D}_s\sigma(r,X_r)\mathrm{d}W_r = 2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]
Owing to the simplicity of the problem, an appropriate solution is of course:
\[
\sigma(s,X_s) = 2 W_s \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]
as we have only allowed a diffusion term, and no drift, i.e., we can write:
\[
2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) = 2 W_s \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) + \int_s^T 2 \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(r)\mathrm{d} W_r
\]
which is of course ridiculous looking, and the second term is just 0. Another way to look at this is:
\[
1 = \frac{\mathbf{D}_s F - \int_s^T \mathbf{D}_s\sigma(r,X_r)\mathrm{d}W_r}{\sigma(s,X_s)}
\]
In slight generality, the above can of course be done restricting ourselves to arbitrary polynomials of \(W_t\), and is a good strategy for a certain class of functions.
Further, we can use some nice properties of Hermite polynomials as follows (Gjessing et al. 1992). Let’s say I can expand a stochastic process \(X_t\) as the linear combination of Hermite Polynomials (for now the specifics are not important, just call them \(H_n(x)\)):
\[
X_t = \sum_{n=0}^N c_n H_n (W_t/\sqrt{t})
\]
where we have plugged in \(W_t/\sqrt{t}\) into its argument to make calculations nice. We then have the beautiful result that with a simple calculation of Stochastic Derivatives, and a result you’ll need to take my word for that works whenever the \(c_n\) are constants, we have:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{c_n}{\sqrt{t}} H_{n-1} (\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)W_t/\sqrt{t})
\]
\[
\delta(\mathbf{D}_s X_t) = C + \sum_{n=1}^N c_n H_n (W_t/\sqrt{t}) = \sum_{n=0}^N c_n H_n (W_t/\sqrt{t})
\]
where here we just identify the initial condition \(C = c_0 H_0 (W_t/\sqrt{t}) = \mathbb{E}[X_t]\), where once again \(\delta(\cdot)\) is here the Skorohod integral, which for adapted predictable functions is the standard Itô (Di Nunno et al. 2009).
Thus a reasonable approach to all our problems is restricting ourselves to the class of finite term Hermite Expandable processes. These polynomials are dense in our space of consideration, so infinite sequences are allowable, but the calculations become difficult. We also have the very nice fact that each \(c_n\) can be computed quite explicitly given that \(H_n\) form an orthonormal basis, and we have that:
\[
c_n = \langle F, H_n\rangle_{\Omega} = \mathbb{E}[F H_n] = \mathbb{E}[\partial^n_x F]
\]
For now this may seem unnecessary, as why not just use polynomials of \(W_t\) themselves, but when we allow for time dependent terms, drifting expectation and diffusive terms may be an issue; i.e., as we may allow all the coefficients to be:
\[
c_n \doteq c_n(t)
\]
where now the Skorohod integral is no longer nice:
\[
\delta\left(c_n(t) H_n \left(\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right) \right)= \int_0^T c_n(t) H_n \left(\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right) \mathrm{d}W_t = \int_0^T \left(\frac{c_n(t)}{t^{\frac{n}{2}}}W^{\diamond n}_t\right) \diamond \dot{W}_t \mathrm{d}t
\]
The last equality again for consideration later (Gjessing et al. 1992).
If we instead wanted a general result holding for arbitrary \(t \in [0,T]\), we would need to explicitly calculate out the chain rule as:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^T \sigma_x(r,X_r)\mathbf{D}_s X_r \mathrm{d}W_r
\]
and in further generality with drift, a kind of complicated theorem so that we can try and evaluate \(\mathbf{D}_s X_t\) as:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{D}_s X_t &= \int_s^t \mathbf{D}_s \mu(r,X_r)\mathrm{d}r + \left(\sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^t \mathbf{D}_s \sigma(r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r \right) \\
    &= \int_s^t \mu_x (r,X_r)\mathbf{D}_s X_r \mathrm{d}r + \left(\sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) \mathbf{D}_s X_r \mathrm{d}W_r \right)
\end{align*}
\]
which one could solve by Itô:
\[
Y_t = \sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^t \mu_x (r,X_r)Y_r \mathrm{d}r + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) Y_r \mathrm{d}W_r
\]
or:
\[
\mathrm{d}Y_t = \mu_x (t,X_t)Y_t \mathrm{d}t + \sigma_x (t,X_t) Y_t \mathrm{d}W_t, \quad Y_s = \sigma(s,X_s)
\]
or explicitly as:
\[
\begin{equation}
Y_t = \sigma(s,X_s)\exp\left\{\int_s^t \left(\mu_x (r,X_r) - \frac{1}{2} \sigma_{x}^2(r,X_r)\right)\mathrm{d}r + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r\right\}
\end{equation}
\tag{1}\]
and then as before need to solve:
\[
Y_t = 2 W_t \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]
This might seem kind of silly now in our case. If we look at the two, the RHS is pure drift, so we just need:
\[
\sigma(s,X_s) + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) Y_r \mathrm{d}W_r = 2 \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\int_0^t \mathrm{d}W_r = 2 \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)W_s + 2 \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\int_s^t \mathrm{d}W_r
\]
so a natural guess would be \(Y_r = 2 \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) \left[ \sigma_x(r,X_r) \right]^{-1}\) and \(\sigma(s,X_s) = 2 W_s \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\), which are both kosher as the derivative \(\sigma_x = 2\).
This is not informative but may demonstrate a way to explore alternative methods so that instead of solving one very complicated equation for one unknown we might have a more tractable, lower order problem.
Alternatively we have the funny approach, which is the Clark-Ocone Formula which we will discuss later in more detail (Hairer 2021; Nualart 2019). The idea is that our problem is reduced to a bias-variance trade-off in the functional form we have been using.

Theorem 1 (Clark-Ocone Formula) Let \(F \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}\) and be \(\mathcal{F}_T\)-measurable (generated by Wiener), i.e.:
\[
\|F\|_{1,2}^2 = \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T F^2 \mathrm{d}t \right] + \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (\mathbf{D}_t F)^2 \mathrm{d}t \right] < \infty
\]
Then:
\[
F = \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t
\]

title: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
section: Critiques after discussion with Nicolas Garcia Trillos
text:
Critiques after discussion with Nicolas Garcia Trillos
I had a short (2 hours haha) meeting with Nicolas, and he came to the probably accurate conclusion that he didn’t feel anything could come out of this “Calculus” other than some heuristics, proof methods, and explicit formulas.
As we have shown above, we can derive necessary conditions for stationary solutions to our functional; however, he was pessimistic regarding whether one could actually equip this procedure with an associated geometry, and from there do something like Gradient Descent.
The hang-ups seemed to be that for any other variation than on the drift by \(\varepsilon \gamma_t\), it may not in any way distinguish a good “Manifold” by which to describe the geometry of the underlying process. The Cameron-Martin Space seems to be a flat and nice-ish place (implied by this drift variation) to consider this, but variation of \(\sigma\) does not seem to have an obvious interpretation.
An idea discussed is how one might impose a metric on a slightly more general space. Say we consider the family of \(P_\theta\) a curve in our space of interest. How do we take our ideas thus far, and translate a “directional derivative” to tangent vectors on this space?
As such, for the rest of the paper we will now do small explorations and elaborations on motivated topics, and the follow-up will be supplementary material such as Wick Calculus, and both formal as well as definitional treatments of Malliavin Calculus.

title: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Bayes-like Perturbations
A silly thing that jumps to my mind is to forcefully be a Bayesian. Consider the following grouping of function and distribution for an underlying parameter. We’d like to ask, how does \(F(X_t)\) change under variation of this underlying \(\theta_t\)?
\[
F(X_t), \quad X_t \sim P_{\theta_t}, \quad \theta_t \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\vartheta_t, \int_0^t v_s \mathrm{d}s\right)
\]
For now let’s just assume that we have absolute continuity with respect to the Lebesgue measure, that \(X_t\) is Markov, and can rewrite using \(G\) as the conditional cumulative distribution function (conditioning on \(\theta_t\); by assumption continuous and differentiable, \(U\) independent of \(\theta_t\) and uniformly distributed) as:
\[
X_t = G^{-1}(t, U, \theta_t)
\]
Therefore let us first consider the Stochastic derivative \(\mathbf{D}_\gamma X_t\), and let the notation \(\Sigma_t \gamma = \int_0^t \sigma_s \dot{\gamma}_s \mathrm{d}s\):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{D}_s X_t &= \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left(G^{-1}(t,U,\theta_t + \varepsilon \Sigma_t\gamma) - G^{-1}(t,U,\theta_t) \right) \\
    &= (G^{-1})' (t,U, \theta_t) \Sigma_t \gamma \\
    &= \frac{\Sigma_t\gamma}{g(G^{-1}(t,U, \theta_t))} \\
    &= \int_0^s \frac{\sigma_r}{g(G^{-1}(r,U, \theta_r))} \dot{\gamma}_r \mathrm{d}r \\
    &= \int_0^T \frac{\sigma_r \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(r)}{g(G^{-1}(r,U, \theta_r))} \dot{\gamma}_r \mathrm{d}r \\
    &= \left \langle \frac{\sigma_r \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(r)}{g(G^{-1}(r,U, \theta_r))}, \dot{\gamma}_r \right \rangle
\end{align*}
\]

title: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Langevin variation
Let us make this analysis clearer. We will consider in the Wasserstein sense the minimization of the functional (Lambert et al. 2022):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{F}[\rho] &= \int \rho \ln \rho + \int U \rho \\
    &= \int \left(\frac{\rho}{\rho^*}\right)\ln{\left(\frac{\rho}{\rho^*}\right)}\rho^*; \quad U \doteq -\ln \rho^* \\
    &= \mathcal{D}_{KL}(\rho \parallel \rho^*)
\end{align*}
\]
The Wasserstein gradient of this function can be calculated with the definition I used earlier to result in (Lambert et al. 2022):
\[
- \nabla \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta \rho}(\rho(x)) = - \left(\frac{\nabla \rho}{\rho} + \nabla U\right) \doteq V(\rho(x))
\]
and thereafter once embedded in the Wasserstein flow, corresponding to the Fokker-Planck equation, we see (with \(v = V(\rho(x))\)):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \partial_t \rho &= - \nabla \cdot ( v \rho) \\
    &= \Delta \rho + \nabla \cdot (\nabla U \rho)
\end{align*}
\]
Here, identifying \(U = f\) as in the usual optimization problem with goal \(\rho^* \propto e^{-f}\):
\[
\partial_t \rho = \Delta \rho + \nabla \cdot (\nabla f \rho)
\]
This of course corresponds to Langevin Diffusion:
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = -\nabla f (X_t) \mathrm{d}t + \sqrt{2} \mathrm{d}W_t
\]










Let us borrow the formula from Equation 1. For general diffusions with drift \(\mu(r,X_r)\) and volatility \(\sigma(r,X_r)\), the tangent variation process \(Y_r = \mathbf{D}_s X_r\) solves:
\[
\mathrm{d}Y_r = \mu_x (r,X_r)Y_r \mathrm{d}r + \sigma_x (r,X_r) Y_r \mathrm{d}W_r, \quad Y_s = \sigma(s,X_s)
\]
with explicit geometric solution:
\[
Y_t = \sigma(s,X_s)\exp\left\{\int_s^t \left(\mu_x (r,X_r) - \frac{1}{2} \sigma_{x}^2(r,X_r)\right)\mathrm{d}r + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r\right\}
\]
We find that for the simple Langevin process, the first order (Malliavin) variation of a general diffusion \(X_t\), \(\mathbf{D}_s\), is the solution to a specific SDE, and can be written as (in this specific case):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{D}_s X_t &= \sigma(s,X_s)\exp\left\{\int_s^t \left(\mu_x (r,X_r) - \frac{1}{2} \sigma_{x}^2(r,X_r)\right)\mathrm{d}r + \int_s^t \sigma_x (r,X_r) \mathrm{d}W_r\right\} \\
    &= \sqrt{2}\exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\}.
\end{align*}
\] We alternatively see that this is just the exponential of \(Z_t - Z_s\) which we can call the “Ito-Malliavin-variation” of \(X_r\) (with drift and diffusion, the spatial derivative of the drift and diffusion of \(X_r\)). While possible useless, if anything is a fascinating result to consider. I can attempt to rephrase this as “a perturbation in the underlying Wiener process results in a functional perturbation whose order is related exponentially to the accumulated negative curvature along its path”.
So let’s implement this. We know \(V(X_t)\) and \(\mathbf{D}_s X_t\), so to reconfirm the formula before, as there were likely errors, we will also relabel \(U \doteq f\) the target to differentiate it from the current distribution at time \(t\), \(f_t \sim \rho_t\).
We will for the most part be doing nothing new here. If we had ignored the evaluation at \(\mathbf{D}_s X_t\) and replaced this with just \(X_t\), this would say quite nicely that perturbation is observed as the difference in the gradients of the log-densities. Here it is a bit unwieldy, and I have difficulty really interpreting this result:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \left(\delta_\gamma \mathcal{X}_t\right) &= V \mathbf{D}_\gamma X_t \\
    &= V \int_0^T \mathbf{D}_s X_t \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= V \int_0^t \mathbf{D}_s X_t \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \quad (\mathbf{D}_s X_t = 0, \ s \geq t) \\
    &= \int_0^t V\left(\mathbf{D}_s X_t \cdot \gamma_s\right) \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= \int_0^t \left(V\left(\mathbf{D}_s X_t\right) \cdot \gamma_s + \mathbf{D}_s X_t \cdot V\left(\gamma_s\right)\right) \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= \int_0^t V\left(\mathbf{D}_s X_t\right) \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \quad (\text{deterministic, not a function of } x) \\
    &= \int_0^t \left(\frac{\nabla \rho(\mathbf{D}_s X_t)}{\rho(\mathbf{D}_s X_t)} + \nabla f (\mathbf{D}_s X_t)\right) \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= \int_0^t \left(\nabla \ln \left( \rho(\mathbf{D}_s X_t)\right) + \nabla f(\mathbf{D}_s X_t)\right) \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= -\int_0^t \left( \nabla f_t(\mathbf{D}_s X_t) - \nabla f(\mathbf{D}_s X_t)\right) \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= -\int_0^t \left(\nabla f_t - \nabla f\right)\left(\sqrt{2}\exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\}\right) \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s
\end{align*}
\]
Let us now look at this from the other side, i.e.:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{D}_\gamma V(X_t) &= -\mathbf{D}_\gamma \left(\nabla f_t - \nabla f\right)(X_t) \\
    &= -\left(\Delta f_t - \Delta f\right)(X_t) \cdot \mathbf{D}_\gamma X_t \\
    &= -\left(\Delta f_t - \Delta f\right)(X_t) \cdot \int_0^t \sqrt{2}\exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\} \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s \\
    &= -\int_0^t \sqrt{2}\left(\Delta f_t - \Delta f\right)(X_t) \cdot \exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\} \cdot \gamma_s \mathrm{d}s
\end{align*}
\]
Which is almost just the silly and sort of obvious fact that we have just changed the order of differentiation, but we notice that the derivative is exchanged to be internal or external:
\[
V(\mathbf{D}_\gamma X_t) = -\left\langle \left(\nabla f_t - \nabla f\right)\left(\exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\}\right) , \ \cdot \gamma_s \right\rangle
\]
versus:
\[
\mathbf{D}_\gamma V(X_t) = -\left\langle \nabla \cdot \left(\nabla f_t - \nabla f\right)(X_t) , \ \exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\} \cdot \gamma_s \right\rangle
\]
The difference between the two can therefore be written as follows with \(\varphi_t = (f_t - f)\):
\[
\begin{align*}
    [V, \mathbf{D}_s](X_t) = \nabla \varphi_t (\mathbf{D}_s X_t) - \Delta \varphi_t (X_t) \cdot (\mathbf{D}_s X_t) &= (\nabla \varphi_t \circ \mathbf{D}_s - \Delta \varphi_t \otimes \mathbf{D}_s) X_t \\
    &= (\nabla \cdot ( \varphi_t \circ \mathbf{D}_s - \nabla \varphi_t \otimes \mathbf{D}_s))X_t
\end{align*}
\]
The inner part is of course just a measure of second order or higher differences, i.e., approximately a measure of the change in curvature in time as expected.
We can also try for the heck of it to rewrite the RHS of \(\mathbf{D}_s V(X_t)\) as follows, though I am uncertain for what purpose… We will denote \((\mathbf{D}_s V)^*\), only in the final line, as the variation with respect to the target distribution and the other the current distribution:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbf{D}_s V(X_t) &= -\sqrt{2}\left(\Delta f_t - \Delta f\right)(X_t) \cdot \exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f (X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\} \\
    \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\mathbf{D}_s V(X_t) \exp\left\{-\int_s^t \Delta f_r (r, X_r)\mathrm{d}r\right\} &= -\left(\Delta f - \Delta f_t\right)(X_t) \cdot \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r,X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\} \\
    &= -\partial_t \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r, X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\}\\
    \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{D}_s V(X_t) \cdot (\mathbf{D}_s V)^* (X_t) &= -\partial_t \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r, X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\}
\end{align*}
\]
We now have something that looks like an inner-product:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{2}\int \mathbf{D}_s V(X_t) \cdot (\mathbf{D}_s V)^* (X_t) \mathrm{d}t &= \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r, X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\} \\
    \frac{1}{2} \langle \mathbf{D}_s V(X_t), (\mathbf{D}_s V)^* (X_t)\rangle &= \dots
\end{align*}
\]
Notably, we do not have decay to 0 explicitly as the limiting curvature should be the same, and anything extra comes from random error.
Nicely however, we could use Girsanov’s Theorem to calculate in expectation as we observe that the LHS is only a function of \(X_t\) before the integral with respect to time. With the Radon-Nikodym derivative as:
\[
Z_t = \frac{\mathrm{d}Q}{\mathrm{d}P}\bigg|_t = \exp \left \{\int_0^t \frac{\nabla f(X_r)}{\sqrt{2}}\mathrm{d}r - \int_0^t \left(\frac{\nabla f(X_r)}{\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 \mathrm{d}r \right \}
\]
\[
\begin{align*}
    \frac{1}{2}\int \mathbf{D}_s V(X_t) \cdot (\mathbf{D}_s V)^* (X_t) Z_t \mathrm{d}t &= -\int \partial_t \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r,X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\} Z_t \mathrm{d}t \\
    \frac{1}{2} \langle \mathbf{D}_s V(X_t), (\mathbf{D}_s V)^* (X_t) Z_t\rangle &= \left \langle - \partial_t \exp\left\{-\int_s^t (\Delta f (X_r) - \Delta f_r (r,X_r) )\mathrm{d}r\right\}, Z_t \right \rangle
\end{align*}
\]
The RHS, conditioned on my having gotten the signs for the two terms in \(Z_t\) correct, is now a function of a \(Q\)-Wiener process with no drift, and the two sides are equal in expectation to the inner product not having said \(Z_t\) under this \(Q\)-measure.

title: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization
text:
Malliavin Calculus
The crucial part now is to properly define in what space we live in so we can define a derivative properly (Hairer 2021; Nualart 2019).

Wiener Random Measure
Note, a way to define the Wiener process is as a random measure, acting on some input function. This is how white noise is defined, as a distributional quantity whose aggregate is the Wiener measure.
In the usual way (indicator \(\rightarrow\) simple \(\rightarrow\) dense approximation) we can define:
\[
W[g] = \int g \, \mathrm{d}W
\]
As in the Riesz Representation, this would just look like a functional if we jazz it up a little bit by making the “peculiar” statement that, in some sense:
\[
W[g] = \int g \, \mathrm{d}W = \int g_t \dot{W}_t \, \mathrm{d}t
\]
This is of course informal, but motivates the argument: “well if we can’t talk about regular derivatives, what about functional derivatives?” i.e., this is defined in the weak sense anyway.


Aside/Motivation: \(\dot{W}_t\)
As a motivating example consider \(L^2([0,T])\), a Hilbert space which if nice and separable has a countable orthonormal basis \(\{e_j\}_{j=1}^\infty\) and inner product \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle\).
Let us now define the Wiener process in terms of this orthonormal decomposition as:
\[
\begin{align*}
    W_t &= \int_0^t \mathrm{d}W_s \\
    &= \int \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) \mathrm{d}W_s \\
    &= \int \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \langle \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}, e_j \rangle e_j \mathrm{d}W_s \\
    &= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty} \langle \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}, e_j \rangle \left( \int e_j \mathrm{d}W_s \right)\\
    &= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\left( \int_{0}^{T} \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) e_{j}(s) \mathrm{d}s \right) W_{e_j} \\
    &= \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\left( \int_{0}^{t} e_{j}(s) \mathrm{d}s \right) W_{e_j}
\end{align*}
\]
where each \(W_{e_j}\) is an independent standard Gaussian, and from here we have the usual result that is always abused:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}W_t \doteq \dot{W}_t = \sum_{j=1}^{\infty}e_{j}(t) W_{e_j}
\]
Now, this quantity of course is really not defined in the point-wise sense (you can’t take the derivative of a Brownian Motion), but is something well-defined distributionally in the space.
But remember, what we’re technically taking the derivative with respect to here is the dependence of \(W_t\) on the indicator function \(\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\).


Functional Derivative of Wiener Process

Definition 1 (Malliavin Derivative) Let \(F: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a random variable, \(g \in L^2([0,T])\), and let:
\[
\gamma(t) = \int_0^t g(s) \mathrm{d}s \quad \in \Omega
\]
Then we define the derivative in \(\gamma\) to be:
\[
\mathbf{D}_\gamma F(\omega) = \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{F(\omega + \varepsilon \gamma) - F(\omega)}{\varepsilon}
\]
when it exists, and if even better \(\exists \psi \in L^2 (\lambda \times P)\) s.t.:
\[
\mathbf{D}_\gamma F(\omega) = \int_0^T \psi(t,\omega) g(t) \mathrm{d}t = \langle \psi , g \rangle_{[0,T]}
\]
we say \(F\) is differentiable, and identifying \(\psi\) as its stochastic derivative/gradient we have that:
\[
\mathbf{D}_t F(\omega) = \psi(t,\omega)
\]


Example 1 (Derivative of Wiener Process) The above definition implies that, in the Wiener space where \(W(\omega) = \omega\) is the identity operator:
\[
\mathbf{D}_\gamma W_t(\omega) = \lim_{\varepsilon \rightarrow 0} \frac{\int_0^T \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\mathrm{d}(W + \varepsilon \gamma) - \int_0^T \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}\mathrm{d}(W)}{\varepsilon} = \int_{0}^{T} \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) g(s) \mathrm{d}s
\]
Which implies that:
\[
\psi_s = \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)
\]
as one would expect if I was trying to in general define a kind of anti-stochastic-derivative \(W_t = \int \mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s) \mathrm{d}W_s\). What we have done is not exactly this, but the intuition is good and it’s true when the integrand for the Stochastic Integral representation is a deterministic function.
If it’s not quite correct, we will of course need to cover what is, and this will lead us to developing something called a Skorohod integral where we can show the derivative and anti-derivative comment is true up to a constant (Nualart 2019):
\[
[\mathbf{D},\delta](\gamma, u) = \mathbf{D}_\gamma \delta(u) - \delta \mathbf{D}_\gamma(u) = \langle \dot{\gamma}_t, \dot{u}_t \rangle_{[0,T]}
\]

From here we have many things, for example the chain rule:
\[
\mathbf{D}_t F(W_1, W_2, \dots, W_n) = \sum_{i=1}^n \partial_i F \cdot \mathbf{D}_t W_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \partial_i F \cdot h_i
\]
with \(h_i\) such that \(W[h_i] = W_i\), and a slightly more nuanced fundamental theorem of calculus that would require us to define a new operator called the Skorohod Integral (Nualart 2019).


Skorohod Integral
There are some very beautiful ways to define this object (Wiener-Itô Expansion, etc.), but I will keep this as terse as possible, and only refer back to other representative results as a “bridge” for doing calculations (Di Nunno et al. 2009; Nualart 2019).

Definition 2 (Informal Skorohod Integral) Very simply, the Skorohod Integral can be seen as the adjoint operator of \(\mathbf{D}_t\) in the sense that (Nualart 2019):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_{\gamma}F] &= \mathbb{E}[\langle \mathbf{D}_t F, g \rangle_{[0,T]}] \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F \cdot \delta(g) ]
\end{align*}
\]
Which maps directly to our calculus understanding of divergences (this calculation generally derived via integration by parts on smooth enough \(g\)).

Well, let’s try it! Let \(F = F(W_T)\). Using Stein’s formula for expectation under the Gaussian measure of adapted processes (not predictive) we have, in reverse:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[F \cdot W_T ] &= \mathbb{E}[F' \cdot T ] \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F' \langle \mathbb{I}_{[0,T]},\mathbb{I}_{[0,T]}\rangle_{[0,T]}] \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[ \langle F'\mathbb{I}_{[0,T]},\mathbb{I}_{[0,T]}\rangle_{[0,T]}] \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[ \langle \mathbf{D}_t F,\mathbb{I}_{[0,T]}\rangle_{[0,T]}]
\end{align*}
\]
i.e., we have that:
\[
\delta(\mathbb{I}_{[0,T]}) = W_T = \int_0^T \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
the normal Itô integral. Through the usual way (indicator, simple…), as long as \(u \in \text{Dom}(\delta)\) adapted to \(\mathcal{F}_T\), we have that (Di Nunno et al. 2009):
\[
\delta(u) = \int_0^T u_s \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
In more generality, for predictive (think inside trading, knows before it happens) we have for say the simple process (\(F_i\) an adapted random variable, and \(h_i\) a smooth enough function on a bounded set):
\[
u = \sum_{i=1}^n F_i h_i
\]
that again via integration by parts, or an explicit computation using the chain rule on \(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_\gamma (X Y)]\), we get (Nualart 2019):
\[
\delta(u) = \sum_{i=1}^n F_i W(h_i) - \sum_{i=1}^n \langle \mathbf{D} F_i, h_i \rangle_{[0,T]}
\]
The summand terms are also called the Wick products if rewritten as (Gjessing et al. 1992):
\[
\begin{align*}
    \delta(u) &= \sum_{i=1}^n F_i W(h_i) - \langle \mathbf{D} F_i, h_i \rangle_{[0,T]}\\
    &= \sum_{i=1}^n (F_i h_i) \diamond W
\end{align*}
\]
Thus in the limit as say the partition size goes to 0 we have (in the \(L^2\) sense):
\[
\delta(u) = \int_0^T F_t \mathrm{d}W_t - \int_0^T \mathbf{D}_t F_t \mathrm{d}t
\]
and when \(F_i\) is also predictable (a constant in the projected space), \(\mathbf{D} F_i = 0\), again we recover the normal stochastic integral:
\[
\delta(u) = \int_0^T F_s \mathrm{d}W_s
\]
If you’re interested in further relations, Nualart has some really good material (Nualart 2019) for how the derivative and divergence operator here come up as adjoints with respect to the Gaussian measure, and how the composition of the two is related to something called the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Operator:
\[
\Delta = -\delta \mathbf{D}
\]
Above we have taken for granted the following results:
\[
\text{"Gaussian Derivative":} \quad \mathbf{D}f(\omega) = f' (\omega)
\]
\[
\text{"Gaussian Divergence":} \quad \delta f(\omega) = \omega f(\omega) - f'(\omega)
\]
The latter being the divergence operator also pops up in literature as the “Stein Operator” and is often used to distinguish if something is distributionally Gaussian.
Let’s compose the two via a commutator, and we find that with \(f \in C^2(\mathbb{R})\):
\[
[\mathbf{D},\delta](f) = (\mathbf{D}\delta - \delta \mathbf{D})f = f
\]
In a fascinating manner we can show that the divergence operator is the generator of Hermite Polynomials (we will show later that this is exactly an iterated stochastic integral), i.e.:
\[
H_n(x) = \delta^n 1
\]
where of course \(H_0(x) = 1\). Coming full circle to the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator, we have that the Hermite Polynomials are eigenfunctions/vectors with eigenvalue \(-n\) (Nualart 2019):
\[
\Delta H_n = - \delta \mathbf{D}H_n = -\delta H_n' = -n \delta H_{n-1} = -n H_n
\]
This operator forms a semi-group using \(H_n\) as a basis such that:
\[
P_t H_n = e^{-nt}H_n
\]
This whole bit is stolen from Nualart’s notes of course (Nualart 2019), so the goal is just to demonstrate some properties that make what we’re doing here relevant, e.g., one can show:
\[
f(\omega) - \int_\mathbb{R} f(\omega) \mathrm{d}P_\omega = -\int_{\mathcal{R}^+} \Delta P_t f(\omega) \mathrm{d}t
\]
and that we have nice bounds for smooth functions such as:
\[
\text{Var}(f) \leq \|\mathbf{D} f\|_{L^2 (\mathbb{R},P_\omega)}^2
\]

title: Notes on SDE Constrained Optimization

Asides

Clark-Ocone Formula
From the actual calculations perspective, using Itô calculus makes things “difficult”, and maybe we don’t really like that we can’t solve our equations using the regular kind of calculus. We will introduce what can be called Wick Calculus having many nice properties as a result of Malliavin Calculus (Gjessing et al. 1992).
We can then hope to write our equations in a form similar to a regular ODE or PDE.
As an aside, but very very useful for deriving explicit representations, what we should actually have for adapted, though possibly anticipating, processes here is something called the Clark-Ocone Formula which gives more explicit general justification for what \(\alpha^{F}(W)_t\) should be (Hairer 2021; Nualart 2019).

Theorem 3 (Clark-Ocone Formula) Let \(F \in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}\) and be \(\mathcal{F}_T\) measurable (generated by Wiener), i.e.:
\[
\|F\|_{1,2}^2 = \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T F^2 \mathrm{d}t \right] + \mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^T (\mathbf{D}_t F)^2 \mathrm{d}t \right] < \infty
\]
Then:
\[
F = \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t
\]


Example 2 (Example: \(e^{\sigma W_T}\)) \[
\begin{align*}
    e^{\sigma W_T} &= e^{\frac{\sigma^2}{2}T} + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t e^{\sigma W_T}\mid\mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= e^{\frac{\sigma^2}{2}T} + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\sigma e^{\sigma W_T}\mid\mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= e^{\frac{\sigma^2}{2}T} + \int_0^T \sigma \mathbb{E}[e^{\sigma W_t + \sigma (W_T - W_t)}\mid\mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= e^{\frac{\sigma^2}{2}T} + \int_0^T \sigma e^{\frac{\sigma^2}{2}(T-t)} e^{\sigma W_t} \mathrm{d}W_t
\end{align*}
\]

And note the funny looking expansion if we keep applying Clark-Ocone for suitable functions:
\[
\begin{align*}
    F &= \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_t]\mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}\left[ \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F] +\int_0^t \mathbf{D}_s\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_s]\mathrm{d}W_s \bigg{|} \mathcal{F}_t\right]\mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F] + \int_0^t \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_s\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_s]\mathrm{d}W_s \bigg{|} \mathcal{F}_t\right]\mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_t F] \mathrm{d}W_t + \int_0^T \int_0^t \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{D}_s\mathbf{D}_t F \mid \mathcal{F}_s]\mathrm{d}W_s \mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F] + \int_0^T f_1 (t) \mathrm{d}W_t + \int_0^T \int_0^t f_2(s,t)\mathrm{d}W_s \mathrm{d}W_t \\
    &= \mathbb{E}[F] + \sum_{n=1}^\infty I_n(\tilde{f}_n)
\end{align*}
\]
where:
\[
I_n(\tilde{f}_n) \doteq \int_0^T \int_0^{t_n} \dots \int_0^{t_2} \tilde{f}_n(t_1, \dots , t_n) \mathrm{d}W_{t_1} \dots \mathrm{d}W_{t_n}
\]
and \(\tilde{f}_n\) is symmetric (and therefore not necessarily equal to \(f_n\) as above), are called the \(n^{\text{th}}\)-order Itô integral with the also beautiful result that:
\[
\mathbf{D}_t I_n(\tilde{f}_n) = n I_{n-1}(\tilde{f}_n (t))
\]
which is the way we could have defined the Malliavin Derivative to begin with (Nualart 2019).
Which is rather a consequence of the tools that make Clark-Ocone work, but is a nice teaser at an expansion with respect to iterated stochastic integrals with respect to projections in some sense. An important point here is that these things are awful, dreadful even, to calculate in general and are used mainly as a proof technique rather than for explicit manipulations.
Well let me introduce you to a generalization of the Itô integral, the Skorohod integral which can be seen to be motivated by the above iterated integrals but apply to special cases and differ with respect to predictive functions (Di Nunno et al. 2009; Nualart 2019).


Wick Calculus
We have mentioned before that the iterated stochastic integral \(I_n(\cdot)\) can form a kind of decomposition of a function (Gjessing et al. 1992; Nualart 2019):
\[
F = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} I_n(f_n)
\]
for some symmetric functions \(f_n\) (the “tilde” has been dropped henceforth because it is annoying). One can make these even more explicit by observing, as historically Itô did, that for Hermite Polynomials:
\[
H_n(x) = (-1)^n e^{\frac{1}{2}x^2} \frac{\mathrm{d}^n}{\mathrm{d}x^n}\left(e^{-\frac{1}{2}x^2}\right)
\]
and for a given function \(g(t)\):
\[
I_n (g^{\otimes n}) = \|g\|^n H_n \left(\frac{\int g \, \mathrm{d}W}{\|g\|} \right)
\]
Think of this as making more explicit what one would want to do by writing:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \left(\int_0^t g_s \mathrm{d}W_s\right)^n &\tilde{=} \int_0^t \dots \int_0^t g_{s_1} \dots g_{s_n} \mathrm{d}W_{s_1} \otimes \dots \otimes \mathrm{d}W_{s_n} \\
    &\tilde{=} \int_{[0,t]^n} g_s^{\otimes n} \mathrm{d}W^\otimes_s
\end{align*}
\]
where we can no longer define equality, as:
\[
\mathrm{d}W_s \otimes \mathrm{d}W_t \neq \mathrm{d}W_s \cdot \mathrm{d}W_t
\]
in the sense of preserving norms (Itô Isometry) as well as other properties you would like such as it being a Martingale.
In a similar manner to the above representation, though not as explicitly, we can also write:
\[
F = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} c_n H_n (f_n)
\]
where \(f_n\) has unit norm in \(L^2 ([0,T] \times \Omega)\). So if we treat this as an orthonormal decomposition (each of the polynomials are orthogonal with respect to the Wiener Measure), i.e., we take, considering \(\hat{\otimes}\) the symmetrized product:
\[
I_n(e_1^{\otimes \alpha_1}\hat{\otimes}\dots\hat{\otimes}e_n^{\alpha_n}) = \prod_{k=1}^{n}H_{\alpha_k}\left(\int_0^T e_k(t)\mathrm{d}W_t\right)
\]
which is often called Wick’s Theorem (Gjessing et al. 1992), we have the decomposition further to:
\[
F = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \tilde{c}_n H_n
\]
where \(H_n\) is understood as being constructed from the underlying basis.
When restricting \(X_t\) to finite Hermite polynomial expansions:
\[
X_t = \sum_{n=0}^N c_n H_n \left(\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right)
\]
the Malliavin derivative simplifies to:
\[
\mathbf{D}_s X_t = \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{c_n}{\sqrt{t}} H_{n-1} \left(\mathbb{I}_{[0,t]}(s)\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right)
\] Since Hermite polynomials form an orthonormal basis on Wiener space (Gjessing et al. 1992; Nualart 2019), the coefficients satisfy:
\[
c_n = \langle F, H_n\rangle_{\Omega} = \mathbb{E}[F H_n] = \mathbb{E}[\partial^n_x F]
\]
When coefficients are time-dependent (\(c_n \doteq c_n(t)\)), the Skorohod integral takes the Wick product form:
\[
\delta\left(c_n(t) H_n \left(\frac{W_t}{\sqrt{t}}\right) \right) = \int_0^T \left(\frac{c_n(t)}{t^{n/2}}W^{\diamond n}_t\right) \diamond \dot{W}_t \mathrm{d}t
\]
Now we define the Wick product in the following way:

Definition 3 (Wick Product) Let \(X\) and \(Y\) have the following decomposition (Gjessing et al. 1992):
\[
X = \sum_{\alpha} x_\alpha H_\alpha, \quad Y = \sum_{\beta} y_\beta H_\beta
\]
Then the Wick product is defined as:
\[
\begin{align*}
    X \diamond Y &= \sum_{\alpha,\beta} x_\alpha y_\beta H_{\alpha + \beta} \\
    &= \sum_{\gamma} \left(\sum_{\alpha + \beta=\gamma} x_\alpha y_\beta \right) H_{\gamma}
\end{align*}
\]

From this, we have another beautiful result that (Gjessing et al. 1992):
\[
\delta(X) = \int X \delta W = \int X_t \diamond \dot{W}_t \mathrm{d}t
\]
which can be extended to an arbitrary Lévy process or Semi-Martingale as long as the basis polynomials are defined correctly (easiest way to find them is to find the exponential martingale for a stochastic process and then expand it out term by term, the \(n^{\text{th}}\) order Martingale will be the coefficient of the \(n^{\text{th}}\) power \(x^n\)).
The Wick product is a product in every sense of the word, and works like the product in a normal deterministic integral (Note \(X \diamond Y = X \cdot Y\) when either or both are deterministic).
So when you write:
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = f(X_t)\mathrm{d}t + \sigma(X_t)\mathrm{d}W_t
\]
what you mean is:
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = (f(X_t) + \sigma(X_t)\diamond \dot{W}_t) \mathrm{d}t
\]
Which can be rewritten in the Wick sense (products are now Wick Products) as (Di Nunno et al. 2009):
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} X_t = f(X_t) + \sigma(X_t)\diamond \dot{W}_t
\]

Example 3 (Geometric Brownian Motion in Wick Form) As a more familiar example we can write:
\[
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{d}X_t &= X_t (\mu \mathrm{d}t + \sigma \mathrm{d}W_t) \\
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} X_t &\doteq X_t \diamond (\mu + \sigma \dot{W}_t)
\end{align*}
\]
The equation is solved like the usual ODE but with Wick Product as (Di Nunno et al. 2009; Gjessing et al. 1992):
\[
X_t = x_0 \exp(\mu t)\exp^{\diamond}(\sigma W_t)
\]
where one can show (what term is missing that would make \(\exp^{\diamond}(\sigma W_t)\) an exponential martingale? Well \(\exp(\sigma W_t - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}t)\) is an exponential martingale…):
\[
X_t = x_0 \exp(\mu t) \exp^{\diamond}(\sigma W_t) = x_0 \exp \left( \left(\mu - \frac{\sigma^2}{2}\right)t + \sigma W_t \right)
\]

which allows us, after rewriting, to use the normal tools of calculus.

Ergodicity Concepts
Ergodicity gives us tools to relate ensemble and path-wise dynamics, but is the weakest in the mixing hierarchy: \(\mathrm{mixing} \implies \mathrm{(weak)mixing} \implies \mathrm{ergodic}\). We will briefly run through relevant definitions, which we sometimes specialize for easy of discussion here.

Definition 1 For a measure space \((\Omega,\mu)\) for \(\Omega\) a Banach space and \(\mu\) a measure over \(\sigma(\Omega)\), we call \(T_s : \Omega \rightarrow \Omega\) for \(s\in \R_+\) the transform map of a random variable \(X_s(\omega)\) for \(\omega \in \Omega\) if:

\(T\) is measure preserving: \(\mu(T^{-1}(\Omega)) = \mu(\Omega)\).
\(T_s\) is measureable for all \(s\), i.e. for \(A\in \sigma(\Omega)\), \(T_s^{-1}(A) \in \sigma(\Omega)\), where we write \((\mu\circ T_s^{-1})(A) = \mu_s(A) = \Pr[X_s \in A]\).
\(T_s\) admits composition \(T_s \circ T_{t} = T_{s+t}\)
\(T_S\) is continuous in \(s\), i.e. \(\lim_{h\downarrow 0}\norm{T_s - T_{s+h}} =0\)



Definition 2 We say that \(T\), a transform map is (strongly) mixing for measure \(\mu\) if \[
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{t\uparrow\infty}\mu(A \cap T_t^{-1}(B)) = \mu(A)\mu(B)
\end{equation*}
\]


Definition 3 We say that \(T\), a transform map is weakly mixing for measure \(\mu\) if \[
\begin{equation*}
\lim_{N\uparrow\infty}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\abs{\mu(A \cap T_k^{-1}(B)) -\mu(A)\mu(B)} = 0
\end{equation*}
\]


Definition 4 We say that \(T\), a transform map is ergodic for measure \(\mu\) if:

\(T\) is measure preserving: \(\mu(T^{-1}(\Omega)) = \mu(\Omega)\)
If \(J\) is an invariant map of \(T\), i.e. \(T^{-1}(J) = J\), then \(\mu(J) \in \cbr{0,1}\).



This statement implies that \(J\) must be either “essentially” the entire space (\(\mu(\Omega) = 1\)) or “essentially” nothing (\(\mu(\phi) = 0\)); in either case the difference between \(J\) and the two options is of size or measure zero - e.g. maybe a countable number of points for example.3
3 This, as already indicated, identifies that once a random variable \(X_s \in J\) (associated to our probability measure \(\mu_s\)), it is in there forever with probability 1: if \(\mu(T_s^{-1}J) = 0\) then almost all \(X_s\) with probability \(1\) are never in \(J\) if initialized with distribution \(\mu\) (note \(T_0\) is the identify map by the continuity assumption). This is just a reiteration of the invariance under the forward map, \(\Pr[X_s \in J] = \mu(T_s^{-1}J) = \mu(J)\in \cbr{0,1}\), plus the measure preserving property and definition of ergodicity.We note that ergodic random variables \(X_s\) (those constructed via an ergodic map: \(X_{s+t} = T_t (X_s)\)), by construction identify \(\mu\) as their stationary distribtion, i.e. \(\lim_{t\uparrow\infty}\mu \circ T_s^{-1} = \mu\) where instead simply \(\mu_s = \mu_t\) for all \(s,t\ge 0\). Ergodicity is a stricter form of stationarity (finer). The distiction needed to be made here is the exact initial position \(X_s\).
We will assume that \(X_0(\omega)=\omega\), i.e. we do not start observing all paths, observable in aggregate with \(\mu\), but observe the specific process \(\pr{X_s(\omega)}_{s \ge 0}\) with distribution path \[
\mu_s^{\omega}\doteq\pr{\mu_s\circ \delta_\omega}_{s \ge 0}
\] which is not stationary. Written this way, it is still deceiving, as the distribution path \(\mu_s^{\omega}\) is still about an ensemble given a starting position, not the path \(X_s(\omega)\) itself (which may be completely determined by an individual \(\omega\)).4
4 In the previous section’s discussion, we should note that stationarity and ergodicity in time are equivalent to invariance of \((\Sigma_k)_{k\in \Z}\) under displacement in time \(T_n(\Sigma_k)_{k\in \Z} = (\Sigma_{k+n})_{k\in \Z} \deq (\Sigma_{k})_{k\in \Z}\). Here we are again with respect to the simple random walk, with all its other problems, we have a non-stationary process where \(\Sigma_0 = 0\), i.e. \(\mu_k^{0}\).5 That \(X\sim \mu\) further stipulates that we cannot look at any ensemble initialized on say \(A\), with corresponding measure path \(\mu_s^{A}\) but that we also need to wait long enough that \(\mu_s^A \approx \mu\). This begs the question of whether the current ensemble, potentially as it evolves, is a good representative sample to measure from in order to estimate our paths, as in practice (imagining \(A\) as a discrete set of points; a physical population) we estimate \[
\begin{equation*}
  \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T}f\pr{X_t(\omega)} \approx \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T}\E[f(X_t^A)] \approx \E[f(X)].
\end{equation*}
\] The stipulation here is that eventually all paths and the ensemble “look” alike, you could even “substitute” one for the other as representative for the same individual at different point in their life.The primary observation of Ergodic theory is that there is information about all individual paths observable (measurable) from the ensemble, if we watch the ensemble for a long enough time. Here, we have what is called Birkoff’s theorem, indicating that for almost any initialization of \(X_s(\omega)\) (with associated measure and ergodic map) \[
\begin{equation*}
  \lim_{T\uparrow\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=0}^{T}f\pr{X_t} = \E[f(X)], \quad \mathrm{a.s}.
\end{equation*}
\] where \(X\) identifies the distributional limit of \(X_t\), or rather \(X\sim \mu\), for stationary measure \(\mu\). Here the identification that this result is almost sure is why this is often called the “Point-wise Ergodic Theorem”, which say for almost all but a size 0 set of paths, the time average converges to a deterministic value corresponding to the ensemble average for the function (generalization of law of large numbers). 5
As an example application (which will lead up to further discussion), consider
\[
N(t,A) = \lambda\{s : X_s \in A, s \in [0,t]\},
\]
understood as the “amount of time, \(X_s\) is in \(A\)” (\(\lambda\) is the Lebesgue measure which is just the length of the set in the traditional sense \(\lambda [0,t) = t\)). Then by Birkoff’s we have that
\[
\lim_{t\rightarrow \infty} \frac{N(t,A)}{t} = \Pr[X \in A] = \mu(A),
\]
which says that the amount of time spent in set \(A\) is equal to the probability that any path might be in \(A\) if we wait long enough (basically forget the limit and approximate).6 7
6 Under ergodicity, we see that if \(\mu(J)= 1\) then \(\Pr[X \in A] = \Pr[X \in A \cap J]\).7 An informal, view of Birkoffs essentially indicates that if we scramble time and take the average under permutation (sample time average) and treat it as if it was from an ensemble (sample population average), the usual law of large numbers for sample means holds \[
\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} f(X_s)\dd s &\approx \frac{1}{T} \sum_{j=0}^{N-1} f(X_{s_j}) \Delta s_j \\
&= \frac{1}{T} \sum_{j=0}^{T-1} f(X_{s_{\pi(j)}}) \Delta s_{\pi(j)} \\
&\approx \E[f(X_1)]
\end{align*}
\] where \(\pi (\cdot)\) is a permutation of all possible rational numbers \(s_j \in \Q \cap [0,T]\) (note: we are considering a countably dense set of points), where we may assume for instance that we are taking “finer” partitions as \(N\uparrow \infty\); we can just take \(\Delta s_i = 1/N\) in the simplest case.
Extentions of Birkoff
In Ergodic theory, what you can discuss are things called Ergodic Components. Basically say you have spaces \((T,J_1,J_2)\) where these spaces don’t connect to one another except from \(T \rightarrow J_j\) (\(T\) is the “transitive space”, basically you eventually leave, unless the process is ugly) and once in \(J_j\) you never leave (at least not in probability). These \(J_j\) could be absorbing states, or might be richer sets, but at the end of the day, instead of using Birkhoff’s in the traditional sense, we can extend this to the Birkhoff-Khinchin which augments Birkhoff as follows8, again defining \(N(t,A) = \lambda\{s : X_s \in A, s \in [0,t]\}\),
8 Importantly, any ergodic measure \(\mu\) can be represented as a decomposition over its ergodic components, with \[
\mu = \rho \mu^{J_1} + (1-\rho)\mu^{J_2}
\] where \(\rho = \Pr[X_s \text{ is eventually in } J_1]\) (note: the transient part is missing; there is no \(\mu^T\), as with probability \(1\) all paths eventually leave \(T\)). This extends to more general parameterizations, where for ergodic components identified with parameter \(\theta \in\Theta\) \[
\mu(A) = \int_\Theta \mu^{\theta}(A) \dd \rho(\theta).
\]\[
\mathbb{E}[f(X)| J_j] = \pr{\lim_{T\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{N(T,J_j)} \int_{0}^{T} f(X_s)\mathbb{I}_{X_s \in J_j} \dd s} \quad \text{a.s.}
\]
which complicated expression just indicating that conditioned on being in \(J_j\), then Birkhoff holds with \(\mu^{J_j}\) (if you’re in an Ergodic component \(\implies\) you’re Ergodic!). This identifies the asymptotic quantity itself as random variables, specifically9 \[
\begin{align*}
    \lim_{T\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} f(X_s)\dd s &= \mathbb{E}[f(X)| J_j] \\
    &\text{w.p} \quad\Pr[X_s \ \text{eventually in } J_j]
\end{align*}
\]
9 We remember here that \(N(t,A)/t \rightarrow \Pr[X\in A]\). Defining \[
\cbr{Y_s : s \in [0,N(T,J_j)]} =\mathrm{Join}\cbr{X_s : X_s \in J_j, s \in [0,T]}
\] as a simply reordering/joining of the process \(X_s\) such that that \(X_s \in J_j\); which can approximate in as having times \(s \in [0,T\Pr[X\in J_j]]\); a change of variables in time induces the same space $[0,T]. By definition, we observe that \(\E[f(Y_s)/\Pr[X \in J_j]] = \E[\cbr{X_s | X_s \in J_j}\). We therefore find the stated fact (in approximation): \[
\begin{align*}
  \frac{1}{N(T,J_j)} \int_{0}^{T} f(X_s)\mathbb{I}_{X_s \in J_j} \dd s
  &= \frac{1}{N(T,J_j)} \int_{0}^{N(T,J_j)} f(X_s)\mathbb{I}_{X_s \in J_j} \dd s \dd s \\
  &\approx \frac{1}{T\Pr[X\in J_j]} \int_{0}^{T\Pr[X\in J_j]} f(Y_s) \dd s \\
  &\approx \E[f(X)|\mathcal{I_j}]
\end{align*}
\]Once I say “any point” Ergodicity tells me that there are an overwelmingly infinite number of points after a large enough \(T\) that are essentially indistinguishable from one another (in the grand scheme of things - \(L_1\) convergence sense) and therefore this average should look like an ensemble average; getting closer the larger \(N\) is as it relates to \(T\) (size \(T = \lambda[0,T) < \lambda[T,\infty) = \infty, \implies\) “uniform sampling” of points for my average gives \(0\) points coming from \([0,T]\) with probability 1).

Commentary
These prior statements deal with the “long-time” dynamics of this process \(f(X_s)\), presuming that the variability of averages are vanishing. In practice however, this observation is just that the error of our time averages is “small enough” after some large time \(T\) with respect to our ensemble average and that they are consistent across paths (tending to the same quantity for most paths). Essentially, “our estimates are stable and descriptive”, and “our estimates apply equally to populations, and as well as across an individuals life”: that we may transfer ensemble dynamics to path-wise dynamics. Ergodicity give us information the properties of path ensembles of paths. This information is not restricted to infinite time as required by Birkhoff (\(T\rightarrow\infty)\) but has value also in medium or short (finite) time processes, but depends on how representative the population is for the individual. How “representative” will depend on the distribution of the ensemble, specifically how close this distribution approximates the stationary distribution. Temporally, we will care about how long we have observed the individual and the population, asking whether each has had enough time to explore the space; note that if all individuals behave the same, the more coverage we will have (in time and space) of a single individuals life (which we can think of as being approximated by others “close to them” in the population).
In the rest of these notes I will cover some related concepts and at the end include some questions of consideration (either that they were or are being considered by the author). We will begin with a small off-shoot to talking about mixing times, which will attempt to give an answer to “have we watched/measured the individual long enough?” assuming that the population is stationary and the individual dynamic. Afterwards we will discuss the premise of using ergodicity for decisions. Specifically, we will discuss “growth-rate optimality” which is the premise of Ergodicity Economics. This will be the primary (potentially temporary) interest of these notes, attempting to clarify and account for related concepts; as well as being a dumping ground for some superficial analysis.

Consequence: Ruin under AGRM Indistinguishably
The premise for this section is simple: AGRM does not distinguish between differences in volatility subject to the same asymptotic growth-rate.14 This is expressly do to the assumption of not finite time horizon; if you play forever, who cares as long as your wealth diverges to infinity. For now, I can see two work arounds, potentially in combination:
14 Say I give you two processes \(X_t=e^{r_X(t)}\) and \(Y_t=e^{r_Y(t)}\) with random growth rate increments \[
\begin{align}
r_X(t) &\sim \mathcal{N}(gt,t\sigma_X^2) \\
r_Y(t) &\sim \mathcal{N}(gt,t\sigma_Y^2).
\end{align}
\]
Observe the actual physical time horizon.
Observe absorbing states in association too, or caused by (lack) of wealth.

The first should be clear, we die eventually even without input. The second is premised on the fact that for instance under most multiplicative games, there is no non-asymptotic absorbing state; under sufficiently poor growth rates you will be penniless (fractions-of-a-fraction of a penny) but, as modeled, will never die due to your wealth. Incorporating both is simply specifying a morbidity function \(Q(t,X_t)\) (the literal survival function for time of death \(\tau\), that death \(Q(t,X_t)=\Pr[\tau>t|X_t]\)) which will depend on the current time and current wealth, which will dictate the probability of death at time \(t\).
As a simplification we will for now consider that time alive is valuable without diminishing, and that we would like to maximize it as much as possible. If we wish later to make time less valuable, the clearest way to diminish the worth of time is to diminish the growth rate.15
15 Less wealth accrued over time, means longer times below a certain level of wealth, leading to increased chance of death for instance.The problem can therefore be phrase as “maximizing my growth rate for the longest time” which here we simplify as total growth. For a multiplicative gamble this is just
\[
\arg\max\cbr{\log\pr{X_{\tau_1}^{(1)}},\ldots  \log\pr{X_{\tau_{m}}^{(m)}}}
\] where \(\tau_j\) are determined themselves determined by the wealth process \(X_{t}^{(j)}\) and the morbidity function \(Q(t,X_t^{(j)})\). If we are to parse \(\tau_j\) in terms of expectation, then applying the law of total expectation (condition on the entire path \(X_t = x_t\))16
16 This problem seems to be something we might deal with more directly via an optional stopping time for martingales.\[
\E[\tau_j] = \E\br{\int_0^\infty Q\pr{t,X_t^{(j)}}\dd t}
\]
